fields.Question: A dense LLM serves a single request (batch size 1) on one GPU. Which phase of generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute?
fields.Choices:
Prefill of the prompt
Decode of each new token
Both phases are compute bound
Neither, tokenization dominates
fields.Correct: Decode of each new token
fields.Explanation: Decode produces one token per step, so every weight is read from HBM to do about 2 FLOPs per parameter: arithmetic intensity is around 1 FLOP per byte, far below the GPU ridge point. Prefill processes all prompt tokens in one pass, so each weight read is reused across hundreds or thousands of tokens and the matmuls are compute bound. Saying both are compute bound ignores that decode has no token dimension to amortize weight reads. Tokenization runs on CPU in microseconds and is never the bottleneck for a real model.
fields.Hint: Count how many tokens share each weight read.
fields.Source:
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670)

fields.Question: Which expression gives the KV cache size in bytes for one token of a decoder only transformer?
fields.Choices:
layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element
2 x layers x query_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element
2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element
2 x hidden_size x vocab_size x bytes_per_element
fields.Correct: 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element
fields.Explanation: Each layer stores one key and one value vector per KV head, hence the factor 2 and the use of kv_heads. Dropping the 2 forgets that both K and V are cached. Using query_heads overestimates the cache for grouped query or multi query attention, where many query heads share one KV head. hidden_size x vocab_size is the size of the embedding or unembedding matrix, which is weight memory, not cache.
fields.Hint: K and V, per layer, per KV head.
fields.Source:
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

fields.Question: A model has 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head_dim 128 and stores the KV cache in FP16. How large is the KV cache for one sequence of 4096 tokens?
fields.Choices:
512 MiB
1 GiB
2 GiB
4 GiB
16 GiB
fields.Correct: 2 GiB
fields.Explanation: Per token: 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes = 512 KiB. Times 4096 tokens is 2 GiB. 512 MiB drops a factor of 4. 1 GiB forgets the factor 2 for K and V. 4 GiB assumes 4 bytes per element (FP32). 16 GiB overshoots by 8x, as if every element took 16 bytes.
fields.Hint: Per token first: 2 x layers x heads x head_dim x bytes.
fields.Source:
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

fields.Question: The same 32 layer model keeps 32 query heads but switches to grouped query attention with 8 KV heads. By how much does the KV cache per token shrink?
fields.Choices:
4x
8x
32x
It does not change, query heads are unchanged
fields.Correct: 4x
fields.Explanation: KV cache scales with the number of KV heads, and 32 / 8 = 4. 8x confuses the group count with the reduction. 32x would be multi query attention with a single KV head. The cache stores keys and values, not queries, so keeping 32 query heads does not keep the cache size.
fields.Hint: The cache stores K and V, not Q.
fields.Source: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

fields.Question: During batch size 1 decode with FP16 weights, roughly what is the arithmetic intensity of the weight matrix multiplications?
fields.Choices:
About 300 FLOPs per byte
About 4096 FLOPs per byte, the hidden size
It depends only on context length
About 1 FLOP per byte
fields.Correct: About 1 FLOP per byte
fields.Explanation: Each FP16 weight is 2 bytes and is used for one multiply and one add for the single token: 2 FLOPs / 2 bytes = 1 FLOP per byte. About 300 FLOPs per byte is the ridge point of an H100 class GPU, the intensity needed to be compute bound, not what decode achieves. The hidden size sets matrix shape but each weight is still used once per token. Context length affects attention over the KV cache, not the weight matmuls.
fields.Hint: FLOPs per weight divided by bytes per weight.
fields.Source:
Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model, Williams, Waterman, Patterson (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1498765.1498785)
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

fields.Question: Why does increasing the decode batch size raise throughput almost linearly at first?
fields.Choices:
Each weight read from HBM is reused for every sequence in the batch
Each sequence reads less of its own KV cache
Fewer transformer layers run per step
Attention becomes compute bound immediately
fields.Correct: Each weight read from HBM is reused for every sequence in the batch
fields.Explanation: In decode the cost is dominated by streaming weights from HBM. A batch of B sequences reads the weights once and does B times the FLOPs, so tokens per second grow with B until the step becomes compute bound or KV cache memory runs out. KV cache is per sequence and is not shared, so batching does not reduce it. Every token still passes through every layer. Attention over the KV cache stays memory bound because each sequence's keys and values are used only by that sequence.
fields.Hint: What gets amortized across the batch?
fields.Source:
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)

fields.Question: An 8B parameter model in FP16 runs on one GPU with 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth. Ignoring KV cache reads and overheads, what is the upper bound on tokens per second at batch size 1?
fields.Choices:
About 20
About 200
About 2,000
About 60,000, from peak FLOPs
fields.Correct: About 200
fields.Explanation: Weights are 8B x 2 bytes = 16 GB, and each decode step reads them all: 3,350 GB/s / 16 GB is about 210 steps per second, one token each. About 20 drops a factor of 10. About 2,000 assumes weights are read once per 10 tokens, which only batching gives. 60,000 comes from dividing peak FLOPs by 2 x params, which ignores that batch 1 decode is bandwidth bound.
fields.Source:
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)

fields.Question: Which latency metric is dominated by prefill time for a long prompt?
fields.Choices:
Time per output token
Steady state tokens per second for the user
Time to first token
Aggregate decode throughput
fields.Correct: Time to first token
fields.Explanation: The first token cannot be produced until the whole prompt has been processed, so prefill (plus queueing) sets time to first token. Time per output token and per user tokens per second are set by decode steps. Aggregate decode throughput measures the batch of decode steps across users, not the prompt pass.
fields.Hint: What must finish before any output exists?
fields.Source: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670)

fields.Question: Which part of prefill compute grows quadratically with prompt length?
fields.Choices:
The MLP projections
Computing attention scores QK^T and applying them to V
The QKV projections
The embedding lookup
fields.Correct: Computing attention scores QK^T and applying them to V
fields.Explanation: Each of n tokens attends to up to n tokens, so the score matrix and its product with V cost O(n^2 x d). MLP and QKV projections are per token matmuls, linear in n. The embedding lookup is a gather that is linear in n and nearly free.
fields.Hint: Which step compares every token with every other token?
fields.Source: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)

fields.Question: What is the main reason FlashAttention is faster than a standard attention implementation?
fields.Choices:
It approximates attention with a low rank projection
It reduces attention FLOPs from quadratic to linear
It quantizes Q, K and V to INT8
It tiles the computation in on chip SRAM so the full score matrix is never written to HBM
fields.Correct: It tiles the computation in on chip SRAM so the full score matrix is never written to HBM
fields.Explanation: FlashAttention is exact and IO aware: it computes softmax in blocks with an online rescaling trick, keeping tiles in SRAM and avoiding the n x n reads and writes to HBM. It does not approximate, so low rank is wrong. FLOPs stay quadratic; it even recomputes some in backward. It runs in FP16 or BF16 and does not quantize to INT8.
fields.Hint: It is exact attention, optimized for memory traffic.
fields.Source: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)

fields.Question: When does speculative decoding with a small draft model give the largest speedup?
fields.Choices:
At low batch size, when decode is memory bound and the draft's tokens are often accepted
At very large batch size, when the target model is compute bound
When prompts are long and outputs are one token
When the draft model is the same size as the target
fields.Correct: At low batch size, when decode is memory bound and the draft's tokens are often accepted
fields.Explanation: Verifying k draft tokens costs the target roughly one memory bound step, so accepted tokens come almost free when the GPU has idle compute. At large batch the target is already compute bound and verifying rejected tokens wastes real FLOPs. With one output token there is nothing to speculate; the cost is prefill. A draft as large as the target costs as much as the target and removes the benefit.
fields.Hint: Spare compute is what verification uses.
fields.Source: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

fields.Question: With the speculative sampling scheme from Leviathan et al., how does the output distribution compare to sampling from the target model alone?
fields.Choices:
It matches the draft model's distribution
It is identical to the target model's distribution
Only greedy decoding is preserved; sampled outputs are biased
It is approximate within a temperature dependent error bound
fields.Correct: It is identical to the target model's distribution
fields.Explanation: Each draft token is accepted with probability min(1, p/q) and a rejection resamples from the normalized residual max(0, p - q), which provably yields exactly the target distribution p. The draft only proposes; it never decides the final distribution. The guarantee holds for sampling, not only greedy. There is no approximation error; only the speed depends on how well the draft matches.
fields.Source: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

fields.Question: You must cut the total KV cache bytes per token across the whole deployment, keeping layers and context length fixed. Which change does that?
fields.Choices:
Shard the model with tensor parallelism across more GPUs
Switch from FlashAttention to a paged attention kernel
Retrain or uptrain with grouped query attention
Increase the number of query heads
fields.Correct: Retrain or uptrain with grouped query attention
fields.Explanation: Grouped query attention lowers the number of KV heads, so fewer bytes per token are cached. Tensor parallelism splits the KV heads across GPUs, lowering per GPU memory but not the total. Paged attention cuts fragmentation waste, not the bytes per token that are actually stored. More query heads does not change K and V, and with fixed KV heads it changes nothing in the cache.
fields.Hint: Per GPU and total are different questions.
fields.Source:
GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)
Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150)

fields.Question: A GPU has about 990 TFLOPS dense BF16 and 3.35 TB/s HBM. Ignoring attention and KV cache, roughly what decode batch size makes the BF16 weight matmuls compute bound?
fields.Choices:
Around 8
Around 300
Around 3,000
Never, decode is always memory bound
fields.Correct: Around 300
fields.Explanation: Ridge point = 990e12 / 3.35e12, about 300 FLOPs per byte. With BF16 weights the intensity of decode matmuls is about B FLOPs per byte for batch B, so B near 300 crosses the ridge. 8 is far below and still bandwidth bound. 3,000 overshoots by 10x. Decode is not inherently memory bound: it is at small batch, and large batch serving systems reach compute bound weight matmuls.
fields.Hint: Intensity grows by 1 FLOP per byte per sequence.
fields.Source:
Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model, Williams, Waterman, Patterson (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1498765.1498785)
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)

fields.Question: A server runs decode with batch 128 and 32k token contexts. What dominates HBM traffic per step?
fields.Choices:
Reading the model weights
Reading the KV cache of every sequence
Writing the logits
Reading the token embeddings
fields.Correct: Reading the KV cache of every sequence
fields.Explanation: Weights are read once per step and shared by all 128 sequences, but each sequence reads its own 32k tokens of KV cache, and that total grows with batch x context. Weight reads are amortized at this batch size. Logits are B x vocab, small. Embedding reads touch only one row per sequence.
fields.Hint: Which bytes are not shared across the batch?
fields.Source:
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: What does continuous batching (iteration level scheduling) change compared with static batching?
fields.Choices:
Requests are padded to the same length so one kernel serves the batch
New requests join and finished requests leave at every decode step
Only prefills are batched; decodes run one at a time
The server waits until a full batch of requests arrives
fields.Correct: New requests join and finished requests leave at every decode step
fields.Explanation: Orca style scheduling decides the batch at each iteration, so a finished sequence frees its slot immediately and a waiting request starts without waiting for the batch to drain. Padding to one length is what static batching does and wastes compute. Batching only prefills leaves decode, the memory bound phase, unbatched. Waiting for a full batch is static batching and adds queueing latency.
fields.Source: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)

fields.Question: With static batching, a batch has one request generating 2,000 tokens and seven generating 50. What is the main waste?
fields.Choices:
Seven slots sit idle for most of the 2,000 steps
The long request is truncated to 50 tokens
Prefill is repeated every step
The KV cache of finished requests is recomputed
fields.Correct: Seven slots sit idle for most of the 2,000 steps
fields.Explanation: The batch finishes only when its longest member does, so the short requests' slots do nothing useful for about 1,950 steps. Static batching does not truncate; it waits. Prefill happens once. Finished requests' caches are simply held or freed, not recomputed.
fields.Hint: The batch ends when the longest member ends.
fields.Source: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)

fields.Question: Which problem does PagedAttention mainly solve?
fields.Choices:
Attention FLOPs growing quadratically with context
Model weights not fitting on one GPU
KV cache fragmentation from reserving contiguous memory for each request's maximum length
Slow network transfer between replicas
fields.Correct: KV cache fragmentation from reserving contiguous memory for each request's maximum length
fields.Explanation: Before vLLM, servers preallocated a contiguous KV region per request sized for max length, wasting most of it to internal and external fragmentation. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed size blocks with a block table, like virtual memory pages, so waste is under one block per sequence. It does not change attention FLOPs. Weight sharding is tensor or pipeline parallelism. Network transfer is unrelated.
fields.Source: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: A request asks for 4 parallel samples of the same prompt. How does a paged KV cache avoid storing the prompt's KV four times?
fields.Choices:
It recomputes the prompt for each sample
All samples' block tables point to the same prompt blocks, with copy on write when a shared block is modified
It stores the prompt KV once in CPU memory and streams it
It cannot; parallel sampling needs 4 copies
fields.Correct: All samples' block tables point to the same prompt blocks, with copy on write when a shared block is modified
fields.Explanation: Blocks are reference counted, so sequences forked from one prompt share physical blocks and only copy a block when one of them writes to it. Recomputing the prompt wastes prefill compute. Streaming from CPU memory would make every decode step PCIe bound. Sharing is exactly what vLLM reports as a memory win for parallel sampling and beam search.
fields.Source: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: Which workload gains most from automatic prefix caching?
fields.Choices:
Short unique prompts with long outputs
Random prompts from a public benchmark with no overlap
Single user batch jobs with one prompt each
Many requests sharing the same long system prompt and few shot examples
fields.Correct: Many requests sharing the same long system prompt and few shot examples
fields.Explanation: Prefix caching reuses the KV blocks of an identical leading token sequence, so a shared long prefix skips most prefill. Short unique prompts have nothing to reuse and cost is in decode. Unrelated prompts share no prefix. One prompt per job gives no repeat hits.
fields.Source:
SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104)
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: In a block based prefix cache, what must the key for a cached KV block include?
fields.Choices:
The tokens in that block and all tokens before it
Only the tokens inside the block
The request ID
The block's physical address
fields.Correct: The tokens in that block and all tokens before it
fields.Explanation: A block's keys and values depend on every preceding token through attention in earlier layers and on position, so two blocks with the same tokens but different prefixes are different. Keying on block contents alone returns wrong KV and silently corrupts outputs. The request ID prevents sharing across requests, defeating the purpose. Physical address is where it lives, not what it is.
fields.Hint: KV depends on context, not only content.
fields.Source:
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104)

fields.Question: An LLM server keeps hitting KV cache out of memory under load. What should the admission controller limit?
fields.Choices:
The number of concurrent requests, at a fixed count
Incoming requests per second at the load balancer
Free KV blocks needed for each request's prompt plus expected output
GPU utilization percentage
fields.Correct: Free KV blocks needed for each request's prompt plus expected output
fields.Explanation: Memory demand depends on tokens, not request count: one 100k token request can use more KV than hundreds of short ones. Admitting by available KV blocks for prompt plus an output reservation matches the real resource. A fixed request count still overflows on long requests and underuses memory on short ones. QPS limits ignore request size. GPU utilization is high whether or not memory is close to full.
fields.Source: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: In vLLM, decoding sequences run out of free KV blocks mid generation. What does the scheduler do?
fields.Choices:
Truncates the longest outputs
Preempts some sequences, either swapping their KV blocks to CPU memory or dropping them to recompute later
Evicts model weights to CPU to make room
Crashes with CUDA out of memory
fields.Correct: Preempts some sequences, either swapping their KV blocks to CPU memory or dropping them to recompute later
fields.Explanation: vLLM preempts lower priority sequences (latest arrivals first), then restores them by swapping blocks back or recomputing the prefix. Truncation would change outputs and is not done. Evicting weights would stall every request. A crash is what preallocating systems hit; avoiding it is the point of the scheduler. Newer vLLM releases (V1 engine) only use recompute.
fields.Source: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: Users complain that output streams stall for hundreds of milliseconds whenever a long prompt arrives. Which technique targets that?
fields.Choices:
Bigger max batch size
Disabling continuous batching
Chunked prefill, splitting long prompts and mixing the chunks with ongoing decodes
Speculative decoding
fields.Correct: Chunked prefill, splitting long prompts and mixing the chunks with ongoing decodes
fields.Explanation: A long prefill in one step blocks every decode in that iteration. Chunked prefill bounds the prefill work per step so decodes keep advancing and inter token latency stays smooth. A bigger batch makes each step slower. Disabling continuous batching makes latency worse. Speculative decoding speeds decode but does not stop a long prefill from blocking the step.
fields.Source: SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16369)

fields.Question: A team splits prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools. What is the main new cost they take on?
fields.Choices:
Running prefill twice
Losing continuous batching on the decode pool
Model weights stored on only one pool
Transferring each request's KV cache from the prefill pool to the decode pool
fields.Correct: Transferring each request's KV cache from the prefill pool to the decode pool
fields.Explanation: After prefill the KV cache lives on the prefill GPUs and must move over NVLink or RDMA before decode starts, which needs bandwidth and adds latency. Prefill runs once. Decode pools still use continuous batching. Both pools hold a full copy of the weights, so weights are not on only one pool.
fields.Hint: Where does the KV cache live after prefill?
fields.Source: DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized LLM Serving (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670)

fields.Question: At peak load, p99 inter token latency breaks its SLO while throughput looks great. Which knob most directly trades throughput for that latency?
fields.Choices:
Lower the maximum number of sequences or tokens per scheduling step
Raise the maximum batch size
Increase the prefill chunk size
Turn off prefix caching
fields.Correct: Lower the maximum number of sequences or tokens per scheduling step
fields.Explanation: Each decode step's time grows with the work packed into it, so capping sequences or tokens per step shortens steps and lowers inter token latency at the cost of throughput. Raising batch size does the opposite. Larger prefill chunks make steps longer. Prefix caching saves prefill work and turning it off adds load.
fields.Hint: Step time grows with step work.
fields.Source:
SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.16369)
Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)

fields.Question: Ten replicas each have a local prefix cache, and traffic comes from a few hundred tenants each with its own long system prompt. Which routing policy gives the best cache hit rate without overloading replicas?
fields.Choices:
Round robin across replicas
Random replica choice
Least CPU utilization
Hash the prompt prefix to a preferred replica, falling back to a less loaded one when it is busy
fields.Correct: Hash the prompt prefix to a preferred replica, falling back to a less loaded one when it is busy
fields.Explanation: Prefix affinity sends a tenant's requests where its KV blocks already live; a load bound fallback stops hot tenants from overwhelming one replica. Round robin and random spread each prefix over all replicas, so each cache holds a tenth of the hits. CPU utilization says nothing about which replica has the prefix and is a poor load signal for GPU servers.
fields.Hint: Send requests to where their KV lives.
fields.Source: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104)

fields.Question: When does plain data parallelism (full replica per GPU) stop working on its own?
fields.Choices:
When the global batch is larger than 1,024
When parameters, gradients and optimizer state do not fit on one GPU
When there are more than 8 GPUs
When the dataset does not fit on one disk
fields.Correct: When parameters, gradients and optimizer state do not fit on one GPU
fields.Explanation: Each DP rank holds a full copy of the model state, so DP alone fails once that state plus activations exceeds GPU memory. Large global batches are what DP is good at, subject to optimization limits. DP scales across thousands of GPUs. Datasets are streamed and sharded, not stored per GPU.
fields.Source: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: In Megatron style training on nodes of 8 GPUs connected by NVLink and InfiniBand between nodes, where should the tensor parallel group usually sit?
fields.Choices:
Across nodes, one GPU per node
Within a single node over NVLink
Across racks to spread failures
It does not matter, TP traffic is small
fields.Correct: Within a single node over NVLink
fields.Explanation: Tensor parallelism all reduces activations twice per layer in forward and again in backward, so it needs the highest bandwidth, lowest latency links, which are NVLink inside a node. Spanning nodes puts that traffic on InfiniBand at a fraction of the bandwidth. Spreading across racks is the worst case for this traffic. TP traffic is large and frequent, which is why its degree is normally capped at the node size.
fields.Source:
Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism (https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053)
Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

fields.Question: A GPipe schedule has 4 pipeline stages and 4 micro batches per step. What fraction of the step is bubble (idle)?
fields.Choices:
1/4
3/7
3/4
0, micro batches remove the bubble
fields.Explanation: Bubble fraction is (p - 1) / (m + p - 1) = 3 / 7, about 43 percent. 1/4 assumes one stage idle. 3/4 is (p - 1)/p, which ignores micro batches. Micro batching shrinks the bubble but never removes it in a synchronous schedule.
fields.Source:
GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism (https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965)
Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

fields.Question: Which change reduces the pipeline bubble fraction while keeping the same model and global batch?
fields.Choices:
Add more pipeline stages
Use fewer, larger micro batches
Use more micro batches, or an interleaved schedule with virtual stages
Switch from 1F1B to GPipe scheduling
fields.Correct: Use more micro batches, or an interleaved schedule with virtual stages
fields.Explanation: More micro batches raise m in (p - 1)/(m + p - 1), and interleaving gives each GPU several model chunks so the bubble shrinks by the number of chunks. More stages raise p and the bubble. Fewer micro batches lower m and grow it. 1F1B has the same bubble as GPipe but lower activation memory, so switching back helps nothing.
fields.Hint: Grow m, or shrink effective p.
fields.Source: Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

fields.Question: Which ZeRO stage shards the parameters themselves across data parallel ranks?
fields.Choices:
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
None, ZeRO only shards optimizer state
fields.Correct: Stage 3
fields.Explanation: Stage 1 shards optimizer state, stage 2 adds gradients, stage 3 adds parameters, gathered on demand per layer. Claiming ZeRO only shards optimizer state describes stage 1.
fields.Source: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: A 7.5B parameter model trains with mixed precision Adam (16 bytes of model state per parameter) on 64 data parallel GPUs. With ZeRO stage 3, about how much model state does each GPU hold?
fields.Correct: 1.9 GB
fields.Explanation: Full state is 16 x 7.5B = 120 GB, and stage 3 divides it by 64: about 1.9 GB. 120 GB is plain DP. 31.4 GB is stage 1 (weights and gradients replicated, optimizer sharded). 16.6 GB is stage 2 (only the FP16 weights replicated). These are the figures in the ZeRO paper.
fields.Source: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: Compared with standard data parallel all reduce, roughly how much communication volume does ZeRO stage 3 add per step?
fields.Choices:
None
About 1.5x the data parallel volume
About 10x
About 64x on 64 GPUs
fields.Correct: About 1.5x the data parallel volume
fields.Explanation: DP moves about 2 x params per step (reduce scatter plus all gather inside all reduce). Stage 3 does an all gather of parameters in forward, another in backward, and a reduce scatter of gradients: about 3 x params, 1.5x. It is not free because parameters are fetched on demand. 10x or a factor of the world size would come from broadcasting full copies, which ZeRO avoids.
fields.Hint: Count the all gathers and the reduce scatter.
fields.Source: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: PyTorch FSDP with sharding strategy FULL_SHARD corresponds to which ZeRO stage?
fields.Choices:
Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
It is unrelated to ZeRO
fields.Correct: Stage 3
fields.Explanation: FULL_SHARD shards parameters, gradients and optimizer state, which is ZeRO 3. SHARD_GRAD_OP keeps parameters unsharded between forward and backward, which is close to ZeRO 2. Stage 1 only shards optimizer state. FSDP explicitly builds on the ZeRO design.
fields.Source:
PyTorch FSDP: Experiences on Scaling Fully Sharded Data Parallel (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11277)
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: A 1,024 GPU job on nodes of 8 GPUs (NVLink inside, InfiniBand between) trains a model too big for one node. Which mapping follows common practice?
fields.Choices:
DP inside the node, TP across nodes
TP across all 1,024 GPUs
PP inside the node, TP across nodes
TP inside the node, PP across a few nodes, DP across the rest
fields.Correct: TP inside the node, PP across a few nodes, DP across the rest
fields.Explanation: Put the chattiest parallelism on the fastest links: TP within NVLink, PP across nodes because it only sends activations at stage boundaries, and DP outermost because its gradient all reduce can overlap with backward. DP inside and TP across inverts the bandwidth needs. TP across 1,024 GPUs makes per layer collectives span the cluster. PP inside and TP across again puts the heaviest traffic on the slowest links.
fields.Hint: Most frequent traffic on the fastest links.
fields.Source: Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

fields.Question: Full activation checkpointing recomputes each layer's activations in backward. What does it cost?
fields.Choices:
About one extra forward pass, roughly 33 percent more compute per step
It doubles total step compute
Nothing, recomputation is free on GPUs
Lower gradient accuracy
fields.Correct: About one extra forward pass, roughly 33 percent more compute per step
fields.Explanation: Forward is about 1/3 of training FLOPs (backward is about 2x forward), so redoing forward adds about 33 percent. Doubling would mean recomputing backward too. Recomputation uses real FLOPs. The gradients are mathematically identical; only memory and time change.
fields.Source: Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05198)

fields.Question: Micro batch size is 4 per GPU, gradient accumulation is 8 steps, and there are 64 data parallel ranks. What is the global batch size in sequences?
fields.Explanation: Global batch = micro x accumulation x DP ranks = 4 x 8 x 64 = 2,048. 32 forgets DP. 256 forgets accumulation. 512 forgets the micro batch size. Tensor and pipeline ranks are not counted, since they share the same samples.
fields.Source: Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)

fields.Question: With expert parallelism in a mixture of experts layer, which collective routes tokens to the GPUs holding their experts?
fields.Choices:
All reduce
All to all
Broadcast
All gather only
fields.Correct: All to all
fields.Explanation: Each GPU sends a different subset of its tokens to each other GPU depending on router choices, which is all to all, done again to send outputs back. All reduce sums identical shaped tensors, the DP gradient pattern. Broadcast sends one buffer to everyone. All gather would give every GPU every token and waste the sparsity.
fields.Hint: Each GPU sends different data to each peer.
fields.Source: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668)

fields.Question: A 70B parameter model in FP16 is served with tensor parallelism on 80 GB GPUs. TP degree must be a power of two and weights may use at most 80 percent of total GPU memory. What is the minimum number of GPUs?
fields.Explanation: Weights are 70B x 2 bytes = 140 GB. 140 / 0.8 = 175 GB of GPU memory, so 2 x 80 = 160 is not enough and 4 x 80 = 320 is the smallest power of two that works. 1 GPU holds 80 GB. 2 GPUs fit the weights alone but leave almost nothing for KV cache, which breaks the 80 percent rule. 8 works but is not the minimum.
fields.Hint: Bytes per parameter times parameters, then headroom.
fields.Source: How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

fields.Question: A 70B model is quantized to FP8 weights and the KV cache stays in BF16. Which statement about one 80 GB GPU is true?
fields.Choices:
The weights fit but leave only about 10 GB for KV cache and activations
The weights do not fit
The weights use about 35 GB
FP8 weights also halve the KV cache
fields.Correct: The weights fit but leave only about 10 GB for KV cache and activations
fields.Explanation: FP8 is 1 byte per parameter, so 70 GB of weights on an 80 GB card leaves about 10 GB, enough for little concurrency. Saying they do not fit uses FP16 math. 35 GB would be 4 bit. KV cache precision is set separately; quantizing weights alone does not shrink it.
fields.Source: FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05433)

fields.Question: With mixed precision training and Adam, how many bytes of model state are needed per parameter, excluding activations?
fields.Explanation: 2 bytes FP16 weights, 2 bytes FP16 gradients, and 12 bytes of FP32 optimizer state (master weights, momentum, variance) = 16. 4 is FP32 weights only. 8 forgets the optimizer. 12 is only the optimizer state.
fields.Hint: Weights, gradients, master copy, two moments.
fields.Source:
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)
Mixed Precision Training (https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740)

fields.Question: Can a 7B model be fully fine tuned with mixed precision Adam on a single 80 GB GPU without sharding or offload?
fields.Choices:
Yes, it needs about 14 GB
Yes, it needs about 56 GB
No, model state alone is about 112 GB
No, it needs about 1 TB
fields.Correct: No, model state alone is about 112 GB
fields.Explanation: 16 bytes x 7B = 112 GB before activations, more than 80 GB. 14 GB is only the BF16 weights, the inference footprint. 56 GB uses 8 bytes per parameter and drops optimizer state. 1 TB overestimates by about 10x.
fields.Source: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: Training runs out of memory because of activations, not model state. Which change roughly halves activation memory?
fields.Choices:
Switch from Adam to SGD
Halve the micro batch size
Enable ZeRO stage 1
Lower the learning rate
fields.Correct: Halve the micro batch size
fields.Explanation: Activation memory scales with micro batch x sequence length x hidden size x layers, so halving micro batch halves it, with gradient accumulation keeping the global batch. SGD and ZeRO 1 shrink optimizer state, which is not the problem here. Learning rate has no effect on memory.
fields.Hint: What does activation memory scale with?
fields.Source: Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05198)

fields.Question: W4A16 weight only quantization speeds up batch 1 decode a lot but helps little for large batch prefill. Why?
fields.Choices:
Decode is memory bound so fewer weight bytes help, while prefill is compute bound and still runs FP16 matmuls
Prefill cannot use quantized weights
INT4 kernels only run during decode
Prefill is limited by tokenization
fields.Correct: Decode is memory bound so fewer weight bytes help, while prefill is compute bound and still runs FP16 matmuls
fields.Explanation: Weight only quantization cuts the bytes streamed per step, which is the bottleneck in decode. Prefill is compute bound, and activations stay 16 bit, so the math throughput is unchanged and dequantization adds overhead. Prefill can use the same quantized weights. The kernels run in both phases. Tokenization is not the prefill bottleneck.
fields.Hint: Which resource does weight only quantization save?
fields.Source:
AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

fields.Question: A server is limited by KV cache memory. Switching the KV cache from FP16 to FP8, with weights unchanged, has roughly what effect?
fields.Choices:
No change in capacity, only speed
About 2x as many tokens fit in the KV cache budget
About 4x as many tokens fit
Model weights shrink by half
fields.Correct: About 2x as many tokens fit in the KV cache budget
fields.Explanation: KV bytes per token halve from 2 to 1 byte per element, so the same memory holds about twice the tokens. Capacity is exactly what changes. 4x would need 4 bit KV. Weight memory is separate and unchanged.
fields.Source:
FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.05433)
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

fields.Question: A 7B model is fine tuned with LoRA, base weights frozen in BF16. What dominates model state memory?
fields.Choices:
Optimizer state for all 7B parameters
Gradients for all 7B parameters
The frozen base weights, about 14 GB
The LoRA adapters
fields.Correct: The frozen base weights, about 14 GB
fields.Explanation: Only adapter parameters, usually well under 1 percent of the model, get gradients and Adam state, so the 14 GB of frozen BF16 weights dominate. Optimizer state and gradients for all 7B would only exist in full fine tuning. The adapters are tiny.
fields.Source: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

fields.Question: What lets QLoRA fine tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU?
fields.Choices:
Base weights stored in 4 bit NF4, LoRA adapters in 16 bit, and paged optimizers for memory spikes
Pruning half the layers
Training in FP8 end to end
Offloading all weights to NVMe
fields.Correct: Base weights stored in 4 bit NF4, LoRA adapters in 16 bit, and paged optimizers for memory spikes
fields.Explanation: 65B at about 4 bits is roughly 33 GB, adapters and their optimizer state are small, and paged optimizers absorb spikes. No layers are pruned. QLoRA computes in BF16 after dequantizing, not FP8. Offloading everything to NVMe would be far too slow and is not the method.
fields.Source: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)

fields.Question: Why does FP16 mixed precision training usually need loss scaling while BF16 does not?
fields.Choices:
BF16 has more mantissa bits
FP16 has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients underflow to zero; BF16 has the FP32 exponent range
BF16 gradients are stored in FP32
FP16 cannot represent negative numbers well
fields.Correct: FP16 has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients underflow to zero; BF16 has the FP32 exponent range
fields.Explanation: FP16 has 5 exponent bits and BF16 has 8, like FP32, so BF16 rarely underflows gradients. BF16 actually has fewer mantissa bits (7 vs 10). Gradient storage precision is a separate choice. Both formats have a sign bit.
fields.Source: Mixed Precision Training (https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03740)

fields.Question: Writing a checkpoint takes 2 minutes and the job's mean time between failures is 4 hours. Using Young's approximation, about how often should you checkpoint?
fields.Choices:
Every 2 minutes
About every 30 minutes
About every 4 hours
About every 8 hours
fields.Correct: About every 30 minutes
fields.Explanation: Optimal interval is about sqrt(2 x C x MTBF) = sqrt(2 x 2 x 240) minutes, about 31 minutes. Every 2 minutes spends half the time checkpointing. Every 4 hours or more loses on average half the interval of work per failure, which is hours of cluster time.
fields.Source: A first order approximation to the optimum checkpoint interval, J. W. Young (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/361147.361115)

fields.Question: Meta reported 419 unexpected interruptions over a 54 day Llama 3 405B pretraining snapshot on 16k GPUs. Roughly how often did the job fail?
fields.Choices:
About once every 3 hours
About once a day
About once a week
About once every 10 minutes
fields.Correct: About once every 3 hours
fields.Explanation: 54 x 24 = 1,296 hours / 419 is about 3.1 hours. Once a day or week underestimates how failure rates add up across thousands of components. Once every 10 minutes is far too often for the reported numbers.
fields.Source: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)

fields.Question: With asynchronous checkpointing, which part still blocks training?
fields.Choices:
Writing the checkpoint to remote storage
Copying the state from GPU memory to host memory
Computing a checksum of the full checkpoint
Nothing, it never blocks
fields.Correct: Copying the state from GPU memory to host memory
fields.Explanation: Training must not mutate tensors while they are captured, so the GPU to CPU snapshot is the blocking part; the upload to storage runs in the background. Remote write is exactly what moves off the critical path. Checksums can also run in the background. A consistent snapshot always needs a short pause.
fields.Source:
PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint documentation (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html)
The Llama 3 Herd of Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)

fields.Question: A job trained on 512 GPUs must resume on 384 GPUs after losing nodes. How should checkpoints be designed?
fields.Choices:
Rank 0 gathers and saves the full state, then broadcasts on load
Require the same world size and wait for replacement nodes
Save per rank shards with sharding metadata so a loader can reshard to a new layout
Save only model weights and restart the optimizer
fields.Correct: Save per rank shards with sharding metadata so a loader can reshard to a new layout
fields.Explanation: Distributed checkpoint formats store each tensor's global shape and shard offsets, so each rank writes in parallel and a new layout can read the slices it needs. Gathering to rank 0 is slow and can OOM a single host for large models. Waiting wastes the remaining cluster. Dropping optimizer state destabilizes training.
fields.Hint: Store the layout with the data.
fields.Source: PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint documentation (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html)

fields.Question: In synchronous data parallel training on 1,024 GPUs, one GPU runs 30 percent slower due to thermal throttling. What happens to step time?
fields.Choices:
It rises about 0.03 percent
It rises about 30 percent
It is unchanged because other GPUs compensate
It rises 1,024 x 30 percent
fields.Correct: It rises about 30 percent
fields.Explanation: Every collective waits for the slowest rank, so the whole job runs at the straggler's pace. Averaging over 1,024 GPUs assumes asynchronous work. Other ranks cannot do the slow rank's share in a synchronous step. The slowdown is not multiplied by world size; the job is just as slow as its slowest member.
fields.Hint: Synchronous steps wait for the slowest.
fields.Source: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)

fields.Question: How do large training teams usually find and handle a straggler?
fields.Choices:
Raise the collective timeout
Restart the whole job on the same nodes
Add more GPUs so the straggler's share shrinks
Compare per rank step and collective timings, then drain the slow node and resume from checkpoint
fields.Correct: Compare per rank step and collective timings, then drain the slow node and resume from checkpoint
fields.Explanation: Per rank timing shows which rank others wait for; replacing that node fixes the cause. A longer timeout hides the slowdown. Restarting on the same nodes keeps the bad hardware. More GPUs still wait for the straggler every step.
fields.Source: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)

fields.Question: 2,000 workers each download a 500 GB checkpoint from one storage endpoint limited to 100 Gbps egress. About how long does it take?
fields.Choices:
About 40 seconds
About 2 hours
About 22 hours
About 1 week
fields.Correct: About 22 hours
fields.Explanation: Total bytes are 500 GB x 2,000 = 1 PB. 100 Gbps is 12.5 GB/s, and 1e15 / 12.5e9 is 80,000 seconds, about 22 hours. 40 seconds is one copy at 100 Gbps. 2 hours drops a factor of about 10. A week overestimates by about 7x.
fields.Source: Kraken: P2P Docker registry, Uber (https://github.com/uber/kraken)

fields.Question: How do you distribute a 500 GB checkpoint to 2,000 workers in minutes instead of hours?
fields.Choices:
Peer to peer or tree distribution in chunks, so each worker that has a chunk serves it to others
Have every worker retry the central store with backoff
Compress the weights with gzip
Raise the worker count to parallelize the download
fields.Correct: Peer to peer or tree distribution in chunks, so each worker that has a chunk serves it to others
fields.Explanation: With peer to peer chunks, aggregate upload grows with the number of workers, so total time is close to one transfer plus a log factor, the approach of systems like Kraken. Retrying with backoff still funnels everything through one egress. Float weights compress poorly with gzip. More workers make a central bottleneck worse.
fields.Source: Kraken: P2P Docker registry, Uber (https://github.com/uber/kraken)

fields.Question: In a ring all reduce of S bytes across N GPUs, how many bytes does each GPU send?
fields.Choices:
S
N x S
2 x (N - 1) / N x S
S / N
fields.Correct: 2 x (N - 1) / N x S
fields.Explanation: Ring all reduce is a reduce scatter then an all gather, each sending (N - 1)/N x S, for 2(N - 1)/N x S total, close to 2S for large N and independent of N. S is about half. N x S is the naive send to everyone approach. S / N is one chunk.
fields.Source: NCCL tests performance notes (https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

fields.Question: 8 GPUs ring all reduce 10 GB of gradients, and each GPU's link sustains 100 GB/s. Ignoring latency, about how long does it take?
fields.Choices:
0.1 seconds
About 0.18 seconds
0.8 seconds
1.4 seconds
fields.Correct: About 0.18 seconds
fields.Explanation: Each GPU sends 2 x 7/8 x 10 GB = 17.5 GB, which at 100 GB/s is 0.175 seconds. 0.1 seconds sends only one copy. 0.8 seconds treats all 8 copies as serial. 1.4 seconds uses 2 x (N - 1) x S without dividing by N.
fields.Source: NCCL tests performance notes (https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

fields.Question: All reduce can be decomposed into which two collectives?
fields.Choices:
Broadcast then gather
All to all then broadcast
Reduce scatter then all gather
Scatter then reduce
fields.Correct: Reduce scatter then all gather
fields.Explanation: Reduce scatter leaves each rank with one fully summed shard, and all gather gives everyone every shard. ZeRO and FSDP use the halves separately. Broadcast then gather and scatter then reduce do not give everyone the sum. All to all permutes data without summing.
fields.Hint: ZeRO uses the two halves separately.
fields.Source:
NCCL collective operations (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/collectives.html)
ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)

fields.Question: A ring all reduce spans 16 nodes with 8 GPUs each, NVLink inside nodes (about 900 GB/s per GPU) and 400 Gbps InfiniBand per GPU between nodes. What sets its speed?
fields.Choices:
NVLink bandwidth
PCIe bandwidth to the CPU
The InfiniBand links between nodes, about 50 GB/s per GPU
GPU HBM bandwidth
fields.Correct: The InfiniBand links between nodes, about 50 GB/s per GPU
fields.Explanation: A ring runs at its slowest link, and 400 Gbps is about 50 GB/s, roughly 9x slower than NVLink per direction, so inter node hops dominate. That is why hierarchical algorithms reduce inside the node first. NVLink is the fast part. With GPUDirect RDMA, traffic does not go through the CPU over PCIe as the bottleneck. HBM is far faster than either network.
fields.Hint: The slowest hop in the ring.
fields.Source:
NCCL tests performance notes (https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)
NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)

fields.Question: How does PyTorch DDP hide gradient all reduce time?
fields.Choices:
It skips all reduce on most steps
It sends gradients only after backward finishes, in one big message
It compresses gradients to 1 bit
It groups gradients into buckets and all reduces each bucket as soon as it is ready during backward
fields.Correct: It groups gradients into buckets and all reduces each bucket as soon as it is ready during backward
fields.Explanation: Gradients for later layers are ready first, so DDP launches a bucket's all reduce while backward continues on earlier layers. Skipping all reduce would change the algorithm (that is local SGD). One message at the end exposes all communication. Compression is an optional hook, not the default.
fields.Source: PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.15704)

fields.Question: For small all reduce messages across thousands of GPUs, why do libraries like NCCL often prefer tree algorithms over ring?
fields.Choices:
Ring latency grows linearly with GPU count while tree latency grows logarithmically
Trees send fewer bytes for large messages
Rings cannot span multiple nodes
Trees do not need a reduction operation
fields.Correct: Ring latency grows linearly with GPU count while tree latency grows logarithmically
fields.Explanation: A ring takes 2(N - 1) sequential steps, so at small sizes the per step latency term dominates; a tree needs about log N steps. For large messages ring is bandwidth optimal, so trees do not win on bytes. Rings span nodes routinely. Trees still reduce, they just combine values along the tree.
fields.Source: NCCL tests performance notes (https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

fields.Question: Design an LLM inference API for a 70B model with streaming responses, continuous batching and a p99 time to first token target.
fields.Answer:
Shape: Gateway (auth, rate limits by tokens, not requests) to a router to model replicas. Each replica runs TP across one node and a scheduler with continuous batching over a paged KV cache.

Admission: Admit by free KV blocks for prompt plus reserved output; queue with deadlines; preempt by swap or recompute when blocks run out.

Latency: Chunked prefill so long prompts do not stall decodes; cap tokens per step for inter token latency; consider separate prefill and decode pools if TTFT and ITL fight.

Efficiency: Prefix caching with prefix affinity routing, FP8 weights and KV if quality allows, speculative decoding at low load.

Ops: Metrics for TTFT, ITL, queue depth, KV utilization, preemptions; autoscale on queued tokens; drain replicas before deploys; stream over SSE with resumable cancellation.
fields.Hint: Start from the scarce resource: KV cache memory.
fields.Source:
Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)
Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)
PracHub Anthropic software engineer interview guide (https://prachub.com/interview-guide/anthropic-software-engineer-interview-guide)

fields.Question: Design a platform for running multi week training jobs on thousands of GPUs.
fields.Answer:
Scheduling: Gang scheduling of whole jobs, topology aware placement (TP inside nodes, PP and DP across a rail optimized fabric), quotas and preemption between teams.

Parallelism config: Users declare model and batch; the platform picks TP, PP, DP and ZeRO or FSDP sharding to fit memory and bandwidth.

Reliability: Async sharded checkpoints at a Young interval, hot spare nodes, health checks before admission, straggler detection from per rank timings, automatic drain and restart from the last checkpoint with resharding.

Data: Deterministic sharded data loaders whose position is in the checkpoint so restarts do not repeat or skip data.

Observability: Loss and throughput dashboards, MFU, per rank collective timing, NCCL error triage.
fields.Hint: Failures are the common case at this scale.
fields.Source:
The Llama 3 Herd of Models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)
Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM (https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)
PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint documentation (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html)

fields.Question: Design a system that ships a new 500 GB checkpoint to thousands of inference workers within minutes.
fields.Answer:
Problem: A central store's egress is the bottleneck: 1 PB over 100 Gbps takes about a day.

Approach: Split the checkpoint into content addressed chunks. A tracker hands out peers; workers fetch chunks from peers and the origin, then serve what they have (BitTorrent style, as in Uber Kraken). Prefer peers in the same rack, cache per rack or zone.

Correctness: Per chunk hashes and a signed manifest; a worker only swaps to the new version when all chunks verify.

Rollout: Stage to a canary set, then broadcast; keep the old version until the new one is loaded so rollback is instant.

Load: Stream chunks straight to GPU memory where possible, sharded per TP rank so each GPU fetches only its slice.
fields.Source:
Kraken: P2P Docker registry, Uber (https://github.com/uber/kraken)
PracHub Anthropic software engineer interview guide (https://prachub.com/interview-guide/anthropic-software-engineer-interview-guide)

fields.Question: Design a service that batches GPU inference requests for a non generative model (fixed size outputs) to maximize throughput under a 50 ms p99 latency SLO.
fields.Answer:
Core: Per model queue with a dynamic batcher: launch when the batch hits max size or the oldest request has waited a max delay, whichever comes first.

Tuning: Measure latency against batch size; pick max batch and max delay so queue wait plus compute stays under 50 ms at p99. Pad to a few bucketed shapes to avoid recompilation.

Overload: Bounded queues with deadline aware dropping or 429s instead of letting latency grow; autoscale on queue depth.

Throughput: Several model instances per GPU or CUDA streams to overlap preprocessing, copies and compute; keep preprocessing off the GPU worker thread.

Contrast: Generative models need continuous batching instead, because output lengths vary.
fields.Source:
Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models, OSDI 2022 (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)
PracHub Anthropic software engineer interview guide (https://prachub.com/interview-guide/anthropic-software-engineer-interview-guide)

fields.Question: Estimate how many GPUs you need to serve a 70B model at 100 requests per second with 1,000 token prompts and 300 token outputs.
fields.Answer:
Tokens: 100 x 1,000 = 100k prefill tokens/s and 100 x 300 = 30k decode tokens/s.

Compute: About 2 x 70B = 140 GFLOPs per token. Prefill: 1.4e16 FLOP/s, around 14 H100s at 100 percent, so roughly 30 to 40 at realistic utilization.

Decode: Each 4 GPU TP replica reads 140 GB of FP16 weights per step; at about 13 TB/s aggregate that is about 90 steps/s, so at batch 64 about 6k tokens/s per replica, about 5 replicas, if KV fits.

KV check: With GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, FP16) about 320 KB per token, 1,300 tokens x 64 sequences is about 27 GB per replica, which fits in the headroom.

Answer: On the order of a few dozen GPUs; state assumptions, then refine with measured MFU and bandwidth utilization.
fields.Hint: Split into prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth.
fields.Source:
How to Scale Your Model, Google DeepMind (https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)
NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)
